question: What is the primary advantage of the intramuscular route over subcutaneous administration?

options.A: Painless delivery for all viscous medications
options.B: Complete absence of local tissue irritation
options.C: Zero risk of accidental intravascular injection
options.D: Faster drug absorption due to rich blood supply

explanation: Skeletal muscle contains a dense network of blood vessels that rapidly take up administered drugs. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why would a prescribing doctor choose an intramuscular route instead of the oral route?

options.A: To slow down the systemic effect to several days
options.B: To avoid breakdown of the drug by digestive enzymes
options.C: To ensure the drug remains in the stomach longer
options.D: To make the medication administration entirely painless

explanation: Certain drugs are destroyed by gastrointestinal acids and enzymes, requiring parenteral administration. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h1)

question: Which injection site is safest and most recommended for adult patients?
explanation: The ventrogluteal site lacks major nerves and large blood vessels, making it the safest choice. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h2)

question: Why is the deltoid muscle restricted to low-volume injections?

options.A: The radial nerve runs directly through it
options.B: The muscle mass is relatively small
options.C: It absorbs medication far too slowly
options.D: Skin is too thick in the upper arm

explanation: Small muscle size limits the volume of fluid a deltoid can safely accept without painful distension. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h2)

question: What needle gauge range is most commonly used for adult intramuscular injections?
explanation: A 20 to 25 gauge needle is wide enough for standard medications yet small enough to minimize tissue trauma. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h3)

question: A nurse calculates an IM dose that requires 3 mL of medication in the deltoid. What action is best?

options.A: Switch the route from intramuscular to oral
options.B: Divide the dose and use two different sites
options.C: Use a smaller gauge needle to reduce pressure
options.D: Administer the full 3 mL into the deltoid anyway

explanation: The deltoid cannot hold 3 mL safely, so dividing the volume protects the muscle tissue from damage. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h3)

question: What position helps relax the gluteal muscles during a ventrogluteal injection?

options.C: Side-lying with the top leg flexed

explanation: Flexing the top leg relaxes the gluteal muscle, making needle insertion easier and less painful. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why is pre-injection skin assessment an essential part of patient preparation?

options.A: To determine the exact racial background of the patient
options.B: To measure the exact body temperature of the limb
options.C: To detect lesions or tissue atrophy that contraindicate the site
options.D: To activate local blood circulation before needle entry

explanation: Damaged skin or hardened tissue impairs absorption and increases discomfort or infection risk. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of using the Z-track technique?

options.A: To speed up the absorption of water-soluble vaccines
options.B: To eliminate the need for skin antisepsis
options.C: To seal medication within the muscle and prevent leakage
options.D: To push the needle directly into a major blood vessel

explanation: Displacing the skin creates a zig-zag path that traps irritating drugs inside the muscle tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h5)

question: When should the displaced skin be released during a Z-track injection?

options.A: While the needle is still inside the muscle
options.B: Before cleaning the skin with alcohol
options.C: Immediately before pushing the plunger down
options.D: After the needle has been completely withdrawn

explanation: Releasing the skin only after needle withdrawal completes the seal and traps the fluid inside. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h5)

question: At what angle should an intramuscular needle be inserted into the skin?
explanation: A 90-degree angle ensures the needle penetrates deep into the muscle layer rather than stopping in fat. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h6)

question: Why is a slow injection rate recommended when administering intramuscular medication?

options.A: To cool down the medication before it enters the blood
options.B: To prevent painful muscle distension and tissue trauma
options.C: To give the nurse time to check the patient's chart
options.D: To prevent the plunger from sticking inside the barrel

explanation: Injecting too fast forces fluid into tight muscle fibers too quickly, causing sharp pain and injury. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h6)

question: What safety practice prevents accidental needlestick injuries after an injection?

options.A: Leaving the syringe on the bedside table for later disposal
options.B: Recapping the needle firmly using a two-handed technique
options.C: Discarding the uncapped syringe directly into a sharps box
options.D: Breaking the needle off before placing it in the trash

explanation: Never recapping with two hands eliminates the risk of puncturing your own fingers. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h7)

question: A patient complains of a sharp, burning shooting pain down the leg during an IM injection. What likely happened?

options.A: The subcutaneous fat layer was too thick
options.B: The alcohol prep pad was left wet on the skin
options.C: The medication was too cold out of the fridge
options.D: The needle may have struck or grazed a nerve

explanation: Sharp, radiating, or shooting pain is a classic sign of nerve irritation or direct contact. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h7)

question: When should a nurse document an intramuscular injection in the patient's record?

options.A: At the end of the work shift
options.B: Only if an adverse reaction occurs

explanation: Immediate documentation prevents missed charting and ensures accurate medical records. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h8)

question: Why is a post-injection assessment performed shortly after administration?

options.A: To collect the used syringe from the patient's bedside
options.B: To fulfill mandatory billing requirements for the hospital
options.C: To monitor for local adverse reactions and medication efficacy
options.D: To measure the exact weight loss of the patient

explanation: Checking the patient later confirms the drug is working and no severe local reaction is developing. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h8)
